preamble: Rhotacism of the voiced postalveolar fricative [ʒ] to an alveolar tap. In Slovene and most Croatian dialects, Proto-Slavic *ž became r between vowels in a defined set of words: the forms of *moťi 'can' (moreš 'you can' from *možeši) and the enclitic particle *že, which survives as -r in relative words such as Slovene kdor 'who' (*kъto + *že) and ker 'because' (*jь že). The Freising manuscripts of the 10th century already show both the archaism (ise 'which' < *jь-že) and the innovation (tere 'also' < *te-že). Greenberg (1999) treats it as a sound change whose results were later reversed by lexical replacement in Serbia.

examples.note: Intervocalic ž > r; also in most Croatian dialects.
First attested in the 16th century; the initial k- is analogical.

sources: Greenberg, M. L. (1999). Multiple Causation in the Spread and Reversal of a Sound Change: Rhotacism in South Slavic. Slovenski Jezik/Slovene Linguistic Studies 2: 63–76. https://doi.org/10.3986/SLS.2.1.04
